items.title: Memory Safety Isn't All You Need: Code Reuse Attacks in Memory Safe Languages
items.summary: The paper argues that memory safety removes classic memory-corruption code reuse but not code reuse itself. Attacks such as prototype pollution, DOM clobbering and object injection share one structure: attacker data changes reads of shared runtime state, and the fetched value then drives a sensitive operation. The authors give a language-agnostic weakness-and-gadget framework, a taxonomy of gadget shapes, a systematisation of defences, and a formal model language.
items.takeaway: Memory safety does not stop attackers from abusing shared runtime state, so audit where untrusted input can influence lookups in prototypes, type metadata or the DOM before trusting a language's safety guarantees.

items.title: GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold
items.summary: Google Threat Intelligence Group reports that threat actors have moved from manual prompting to autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks such as PentAGI and CyberStrikeAI. It describes LLM-driven differential analysis of patches to weaponise n-day vulnerabilities at scale, along with LLMJacking that resells stolen cloud AI access and state-linked use of LLMs in influence operations. The update frames these trends as compressing attack timelines against internet-facing systems.
items.takeaway: Patch diffing that once took skilled analysts can now be automated, so the window between a patch release and mass exploitation is shrinking and defenders should prioritise rapid patching of internet-facing systems.

items.title: More Context, Mixed Results: Evaluating LLMs for Identifier Recovery and Code Deobfuscation
items.summary: The authors test three LLMs against traditional baselines for recovering renamed identifiers in obfuscated Java across 51 projects and three obfuscators. Agentic retrieval gives the best identifier detection at 91.56% F1, but exact name recovery peaks at only 16.42% overall, and class names are the hardest to detect. Control-flow obfuscation degrades both tasks more than string encryption, and more context does not always help, particularly for larger methods.
items.takeaway: LLMs help with deobfuscation mainly in detecting what needs renaming, while full semantic recovery remains unreliable, so it is worth choosing context carefully and expecting control-flow obfuscation to be the harder obstacle.

items.title: Agent-ZTA: A chain-Aware Zero Trust Model for Bidirectional Security-State Propagation and Runtime Containment in Multi-Agent Delegation
items.summary: The paper proposes Agent-ZTA, a zero trust authorisation model for multi-agent workflows where an agent's security state can degrade mid-run through upstream compromise or untrusted inputs. It separates path-specific delegated authority from currently exercisable permissions, propagates security events bidirectionally across the delegation graph, and applies branch-scoped containment, including a sandbox mode. The authors give a deterministic decision procedure, five stated properties, and worked traces, and they state their trust assumptions explicitly.
items.takeaway: Static, caller-based authorisation misses risk that appears during execution, so access decisions for agent chains should be re-evaluated against live security state rather than the original delegation alone.

items.title: We Have All the Cards: Securing Agent Cards at the Operational Trust Boundary of the Agent2Agent Protocol
items.summary: The paper examines Agent Cards in the Agent2Agent protocol, where attacker-controlled natural-language fields can steer which agent an orchestrator selects before any invocation occurs. It presents a taxonomy of ten manipulation attacks and SECCARD, a layered validator combining protocol checks, deterministic analysis, and LLM semantic judgement. Measurements across 36.1 million domains and benchmarks show that detection quality varies widely between LLM judges, from 25.8% to 92.3% security recall on the synthetic set.
items.takeaway: Metadata that influences routing or selection is an attack surface in its own right, and any LLM used as a security judge needs its own evaluation because detection performance depends heavily on the chosen model.

items.title: From Bytes to Behavior: Request-Level Attribution from Live GPU Hidden States
items.summary: The authors show that per-layer residual-stream activations can be pulled from a live GPU process with a non-modifying debugger, without knowing the model's architecture or weights. They recovered byte-exact tensors across 33 open-source decoder-only models and trained linear probes on the recovered states, which distinguished refusal from compliance with an AUROC of 0.88. The work suggests live hidden-state acquisition as a new evidence source for examining deployed AI services.
items.takeaway: Volatile GPU memory can hold behavioural evidence about a running AI service that its weights and logs never capture, so forensic acquisition should account for transient tensor state.

items.title: I2C-GRPO: Insight Importance Checklist for Reinforcement Learning in a Multi-Agent DDoS Alert Triage Workflow
items.summary: I2C-GRPO trains a Qwen3-4B agent to triage DDoS alerts by rewarding intermediate investigation steps according to how well they cover ranked forensic insights from an expert LLM panel. The agent reached a mean F1 of 0.869 and a 4.9% false-positive rate on an independent CSE-CIC-IDS2018 trace, against 16.4% for GPT-5-mini. The authors limit their claims to DDoS triage and note that false positives fell only at the highest orness weighting.
items.takeaway: When intermediate investigative steps have no ground-truth labels, a checklist of expert-ranked insights can serve as a proxy reward, but its results should be tested on independent data.

items.title: Can LLMs Write Backdoors? An Empirical Security Study of Weight-Space Programming
items.summary: The authors test whether general-purpose LLMs can edit neural network weights from natural-language instructions to plant backdoors, without training data, forward passes or gradients. Five LLMs were tried across an MLP, ResNet-18 and a fine-tuned Qwen model, and backdoors were injected while clean accuracy stayed largely intact. Some attacks needed as few as six parameters, or 0.02% of the Qwen weights, and only one model succeeded on all three targets.
items.takeaway: Backdoors can be tiny edits to weights that keep normal accuracy high, so model supply chain checks should compare weights against trusted hashes or diffs rather than relying on accuracy tests alone.

items.title: High volume phishing campaign uses Microsoft 365 outage lures to target multiple industry sectors
items.summary: Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed a high-volume phishing campaign using fake Microsoft 365 service-health emails that claimed held mail would be deleted within 24 hours. The messages used rotating sender domains, randomised subjects, recipient-specific tracking links, and a common non-Microsoft destination to evade pattern matching. Credential phishing is assessed as likely, but credential capture and follow-on activity were not confirmed.
items.takeaway: Lures tied to real global events combined with per-recipient links defeat simple pattern matching, so detection should also focus on post-click signals such as new sign-ins, inbox rules, and unusual mailbox access.

items.title: ST-GAT: A Leakage-Free Spatio-Temporal Graph Attention Framework for Robust Network Intrusion Detection
items.summary: The authors propose ST-GAT, a spatio-temporal graph attention model for network intrusion detection that treats traffic as sequences of graph snapshots. They identify two common inflation sources in CSE-CIC-IDS-2018 evaluations, namely overlapping windows that leak future information and preprocessing fitted before the train/test split, and they correct both. Under these conditions, the model reaches a Macro-F1 of 96.65%, about 14 points above a per-flow Random Forest baseline, while balanced resampling hurts minority-class detection.
items.takeaway: Benchmark results for detection models can look strong only because of leakage from overlapping windows or pre-split preprocessing, so check the split methodology before trusting reported gains.

items.title: When the Spec Sheet Lies: Injection Attacks on LLM-Generated Compliance Artifacts
items.summary: The study tests prompt injection against LLM agents that generate industrial compliance documents such as Safety Data Sheets, quality control records and Digital Product Passports. Active falsification instructions succeed most often across scenarios, and success varies widely between models. Models resist passively injected override requests more reliably.
items.takeaway: Compliance artefacts generated by LLMs can be falsified through injected content in source documents, so treat LLM-produced records as untrusted and validate them against authoritative data.

items.title: PrivacyPR: A Dataset of Real-World Privacy Fixes for Benchmarking Privacy-Aware Code Review
items.summary: PrivacyPR is a dataset of 4,131 merged GitHub pull requests that fix real privacy defects, labelled for GDPR principles, with a harness that reintroduces each defect for testing. Two coding agents caught only 42 to 51 per cent of defects under a generic review prompt but 88 to 91 per cent when explicitly asked to check privacy, at the cost of flagging 11 to 15 per cent of non-fix changes. The authors conclude that detection depends strongly on what the reviewer is asked to look for.
items.takeaway: A generic code review prompt can miss defects that a targeted prompt catches easily, so security checks for specific classes of issue should be stated explicitly in automated review pipelines.

items.title: C-to-Rust Translation Validation at the LLVM IR Level via AI-Assisted Refinement Proof
items.summary: R2C2 validates C-to-Rust translations by proving in Rocq that the Rust program refines the C program, working at the LLVM IR level with a common abstraction for data representations. Proof construction is automated by AI agents, but the proof checker removes the need to trust them. Of 519 LLM-produced translations, it proved 486 correct without bounding executions and found three incorrect ones with counterexamples that existing tools missed.
items.takeaway: Machine-checked refinement proofs over a shared intermediate representation can verify translations that testing and bounded model checking cannot, and AI agents can do the proof work safely because the checker validates it.

items.title: Binarization as an Attack Surface in Weightless Neural Networks
items.summary: The authors argue that binarising inputs does not make weightless neural networks robust, because perturbations that cross an encoding threshold still flip bits and change predictions. They formalise this with a threshold-crossing bound and show on MNIST that the encoding granularity trades a small accuracy loss for lower attack success. On Bot-IoT, CICIDS and UNSW-NB15, adversarial perturbations pushed many attacks to normal and raised false alarms.
items.takeaway: Input quantisation can look like a defence against adversarial examples, but any threshold the attacker can cross becomes an attack surface, so encoding choices must be evaluated under adversarial conditions.

items.title: Using machine learning approaches to classify false-positives generated by static analysis tools - An empirical study using small datasets
items.summary: The authors compare code representation learning techniques and machine learning algorithms for filtering false positives from static code analysis tools. They find that the best approach depends on the characteristics of the training dataset and the goal of the model. They recommend further study of simple ML models alongside advanced ones.
items.takeaway: With small labelled datasets, simple models can perform competitively, so test triage classifiers against your dataset size and alarm types before trusting them to suppress findings.
